title: Correlation-assisted spin-selective metallicity in strained and bilayer altermagnets
authors: Marnin J. Di Nunzio, Frank Lechermann, Ilya M. Eremin
abstract: Altermagnets combine vanishing net magnetization with a momentum-dependent spin-split electronic structure, providing a route to spin-polarized carriers without ferromagnetism. Here, we investigate how electronic correlations, doping, uniaxial strain, and interlayer coupling control altermagnetism within a minimal Hubbard-type model for mono- and bilayer systems. Comparing Hartree--Fock theory with the rotationally invariant slave-boson (RISB) approach, we demonstrate the robustness of altermagnetic order against quasiparticle renormalization and reveal a separation between the onset of magnetic order and the loss of quasiparticle coherence at stronger coupling. In the monolayer, doping produces a pronounced particle--hole asymmetry, while its combination with uniaxial strain generates a fully spin-polarized Fermi surface close to half-filling. In the bilayer, stacking that favors ferroic alignment of the layer altermagnetic order parameters allows their momentum-dependent spin splittings to combine constructively. Weak asymmetric doping additionally induces intra-unit-cell charge order, resulting in fully spin-polarized low-energy carriers. At a bilayer filling of five electrons in four orbitals, we find a continuous paramagnet-to-altermagnet transition followed, at stronger coupling, by an evolution toward a Mott-like regime with strongly suppressed quasiparticle weight. Our results establish correlations, strain, doping, and stacking as complementary means of controlling altermagnetic metals and generating fully spin-polarized Fermi surfaces.
summary: This theoretical work explores how various external parameters—such as strain, doping, and interlayer coupling—can control the exotic state of altermagnetism in Hubbard-model systems. By comparing Hartree-Fock and RISB calculations, the authors demonstrate that these controls can generate fully spin-polarized electronic states without requiring conventional ferromagnetism. The findings highlight a rich interplay between structural geometry and electronic correlations in determining magnetic metal behavior.
main_problem: The study investigates how electronic correlations, doping, strain, and interlayer coupling control the emergence and stability of altermagnetism in metallic systems.
main_result: The research establishes that correlations, strain, doping, and stacking are complementary mechanisms to generate fully spin-polarized Fermi surfaces in altermagnetic metals.
method: The authors compare results from Hartree–Fock theory with the more advanced rotationally invariant slave-boson (RISB) approach to treat correlation effects.
model_or_system: The model uses a minimal Hubbard-type Hamiltonian applied to mono- and bilayer systems, featuring hopping terms and an on-site intraorbital Hubbard interaction.
key_observables: Altermagnetic order parameter, quasiparticle (QP) weight ($Z_m$), spin-polarized Fermi surface topology, and charge order.
important_parameters: Interaction strength ($U$), doping level, uniaxial strain magnitude, and interlayer coupling strength.
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on the Hubbard model and the RISB approximation to incorporate correlation-induced quasiparticle renormalization.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the model structure (AA/AB stacking), compare HF vs. RISB results for the altermagnetic transition at half-filling, and show QP dispersions for doping away from half-filling.
paper_structure: The paper systematically analyzes the system by first establishing the model, then comparing mean-field (HF) and correlated (RISB) treatments, and finally detailing the effects of doping and strain in both monolayer and bilayer geometries.
why_interesting: The detailed treatment of correlation effects ($U$) and the comparison between mean-field and slave-boson methods provide valuable insights into the breakdown of simple mean-field descriptions in strongly correlated magnetic metals.
